content: Pityriasis amiantacea was first described by Alibert in 1832. This condition primarily affects the scalp, where it manifests as shiny, asbestos-like (amiantaceous) thick scales that adhere in layers to the hair shafts. These scales encircle and bind down tufts of hair. The condition may be localized to specific areas of the scalp or involve the entire scalp. Repeated removal of hairs attached to the scales can lead to temporary hair loss (alopecia) and, in some cases, scarring alopecia. Pityriasis amiantacea is a rare disorder that predominantly affects females. It is often misdiagnosed due to its resemblance to other scalp conditions such as psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, or lichen planus. However, a distinguishing feature of pityriasis amiantacea is that the scales are firmly attached to both the hair shafts and the scalp. This condition may coexist with other inflammatory skin disorders, such as atopic dermatitis or seborrheic dermatitis, and can be associated with sebaceous scales and alopecia. According to the dermatology reference text Bolognia, pityriasis amiantacea is most commonly observed in cases of psoriasis but may also occur in secondary infections of atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, or tinea capitis. Treatment In the majority of cases, the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus is present. When this bacterium is identified, treatment with systemic antibiotics and coal tar shampoo can completely resolve the condition. Additionally, fungal infections, such as tinea capitis, can mimic the symptoms of pityriasis amiantacea. These fungal infections can be effectively treated with antifungal medications. Diagnosis Physical Examination The condition, sometimes referred to as tinea amiantacea, is characterized by its unique clinical presentation. This terminology and its features are documented in dermatology atlases, which provide visual and descriptive references for accurate diagnosis.
